faq: Is this the same as a penetration test?

No. This is a configuration review and fix, based on common best practice. A penetration test tries to break in and is done by a security specialist. We say so in the report if you would benefit from one.
We test each change on staging or in a quiet window, and we write down every change so it can be undone. The riskiest steps, such as closing ports, are checked against how your app really connects.
We need an admin-level user in your account for the length of the order, which you create and remove yourself. Never share your own login. We list every setting we changed.

desc:
Cloud security hardening closes the gaps attackers look for in your servers and cloud account: open ports, shared logins, loose permissions and secrets in code. Ecom Swift LLC reviews your set-up, fixes what is safe to fix and ranks the rest.

## What is cloud security hardening?

Cloud security hardening is the process of reducing the ways someone can get into your systems. It removes what you do not need, restricts what remains and adds protection around the important parts. The goal is a smaller, better-guarded target, not a promise that nothing can ever go wrong.

Most breaches of small systems do not involve clever attacks. They use ordinary weaknesses: a database port open to the world, a password reused across tools, an access key committed to a public repository or an admin account with no second factor.

## Why default settings are not enough

Cloud providers give you powerful tools, but the defaults prioritize convenience. A new server may accept sign-in from anywhere. A new access role may allow far more than the task needs. A quick fix made during a deadline can stay in place for years.

Over time, a set-up also collects clutter: old users, forgotten servers, unused keys and rules nobody remembers adding. Each one is a door. Hardening is partly a clean-up, because what you no longer use cannot be defended well.

## How hardening reduces business risk

A breach costs more than the technical repair. It can mean exposed customer data, a site that is down, lost time and damaged trust. Hardening lowers the chance of that, and limits the damage if something does go wrong. A leaked key that only has narrow permissions is a small problem. The same key with full administrator rights is a disaster.

It also makes you easier to work with. Customers and partners increasingly ask how you protect data. A documented set-up with clear access rules, logging and a short policy pack gives you something concrete to show. We do not provide legal certification, and the outcome depends on your systems and how the advice is followed.

## What a hardening review covers

- Open ports and firewall rules, trimmed to what each service needs.
- Two-factor sign-in for every account that can change your systems.
- Removal of shared logins, with a named account for each person.
- Least-privilege roles, so people and apps hold only the access they use.
- Secrets moved out of code and into a protected store.
- SSH and admin access limited by key, network location or both.
- Automatic security updates for operating systems and key software.
- Security logging with alerts for unusual sign-ins or changes.
- A vulnerability scan with the findings explained and fixed where safe.
- A web firewall in front of public apps, and a short security checklist for your team.

## How we work

We start with a read-only review of your accounts and servers, noting each risk and how serious it is. We then agree with you which fixes can be made immediately and which need a test or a quiet time. Changes that might affect your app, such as closing a port, are checked with your team before they go live.

You receive a before and after summary and a prioritized list of anything left. The Basic package covers a single server or account with the most important fixes. Standard extends the work to secrets, permissions and automatic updates. Premium adds logging, scans, firewall rules and a policy pack, plus a walkthrough call. This is a hardening and review service, not a penetration test, and it does not by itself certify compliance with any standard.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Give each person their own named account.
- Turn on two-factor sign-in everywhere it is offered.
- Grant the smallest permission that lets the job get done.
- Store keys and passwords in a secrets manager.
- Review who has access whenever someone joins or leaves.

**Avoid:**
- Sharing one administrator password in a chat group.
- Committing keys or tokens to a code repository.
- Leaving test servers running with old software.
- Opening a port to every address to fix a problem quickly.
- Postponing updates indefinitely because things seem fine.

## Who this is for

This service suits a small company that has grown its cloud set-up without ever reviewing it. It suits a founder taking over servers from a previous developer. It also suits a business that has been asked by a customer to show how its systems are protected.

## What we need from you

Tell us which cloud or hosting accounts and servers are in scope and who currently has access. We never need your passwords. Access is given as a read-only or limited administrator user in your own account, and you can remove it when the work is done.
